Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a high‑level “playbook” for how I’d use the two tools you described to place a real‑world order for a burger and fries at McDonald’s. I’ll break it into three logical phases – **Discovery**, **Preparation**, and **Execution** – and show what each phase looks like in practice. --- ## Phase 1 – Discovery (search the internet) | Step | What I do | Why | |------|-----------|-----| | 1️⃣ Search for “McDonald’s online ordering API” | I feed the query into the *search* tool. | Find public or partner‑only docs, SDKs, or community posts that expose the ordering service. | | 2️⃣ Filter results for “public REST API”, “OpenAPI spec”, or “SDK” | I sift through the returned links. | Prefer machine‑readable specs over informal blog posts. | | 3️⃣ Retrieve the best candidate spec (e.g., an OpenAPI YAML/JSON) | I fetch the spec via the same tool or a direct download link. | Gives me the exact endpoint paths, parameter schemas, auth requirements, and sample payloads. | | 4️⃣ Extract key information | I parse the spec to pull out:
• Base URL (e.g., `https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1`)
• Order creation endpoint (`POST /orders`)
• Required headers (Auth, Content‑Type)
• Auth flow (OAuth2 client credentials, API key, etc.) | These are the building blocks for the next phase. | > **Tip:** If the spec is behind a login wall, I’ll look for a “sandbox” or “partner portal” that offers test credentials. Many fast‑food chains expose a sandbox environment for developers. --- ## Phase 2 – Preparation (build the request) | Step | What I do | Why | |------|-----------|-----| | 5️⃣ Resolve authentication | Using the discovered auth flow, I either:
• Call the token endpoint (`POST /oauth/token`), or
• Insert a pre‑obtained API key into the `Authorization` header. | Most ordering APIs require a bearer token or API key. | | 6️⃣ Get the menu (optional but useful) | I call `GET /menu` or similar to list items. | Helps confirm the exact product IDs for “burger” and “fries”. | | 7️⃣ Identify product IDs | From the menu response, I locate the IDs for the specific burger (e.g., “Big Mac”) and fries size (e.g., “Medium”). | The order payload needs numeric IDs, not human‑readable names. | | 8️⃣ Build the order payload | I craft a JSON object such as:
```json\n{\n \"location_id\": 12345,\n \"items\": [\n {\"product_id\": 987, \"quantity\": 1},\n {\"product_id\": 654, \"quantity\": 1}\n ],\n \"payment_method\": {\n \"type\": \"card\",\n \"token\": \"\"\n }\n}\n```\n| The payload must match the schema defined in the spec. | | 9️⃣ Set headers | I prepare headers: ``, `>`. | Ensures the API accepts my request. | > **Note on location:** Some APIs let you specify a store ID or zip code. If the spec requires a physical address, I’ll supply your nearest McDonald’s address. --- ## Phase 3 – Execution (make the actual API call) | Step | What I do | Why | |------|-----------|-----| | 🔟 Execute the order call | I pass the full request string to the *execute* tool:
`POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders`
Headers: …
Body: … | This is the moment the order actually goes to McDonald’s servers. | | 1️⃣1️⃣ Inspect the response | I read the JSON reply. Typical fields: `order_id`, `status`, `estimated_pickup_time`. | Confirms success or surfaces errors (e.g., “invalid product_id”). | | 1️⃣2️⃣ Handle errors | If the status code isn’t 200/201, I log the error message and possibly retry or abort. | Robustness against transient failures. | | 1️⃣3️⃣ Confirm with you | I relay back the `order_id` and ETA so you know the order was placed. | Keeps the user informed. | --- ### Example Flow (pseudo‑code) ```python # 1. Discover spec_url = search_tool("McDonald’s ordering API OpenAPI spec") spec_json = download(spec_url) # 2. Prepare base_url = spec_json["servers"][0]["url"] token_resp = execute_tool( url=f"{base_url}/oauth/token", method="POST", headers={"Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"}, body="grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=XYZ&client_secret=ABC" ) access_token = token_resp.json()["access_token"] # 3. Get menu & pick IDs menu_resp = execute_tool( url=f"{base_url}/menu", method="GET", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {access_token}"} ) burger_id = find_product_id(menu_resp.json(), "Big Mac") fries_id = find_product_id(menu_resp.json(), "Medium Fries") # 4. Build order payload order_payload = { "location_id": 12345, "items": [ {"product_id": burger_id, "quantity": 1}, {"product_id": fries_id, "quantity": 1} ], "payment_method": {"type": "card", "token": ""} } # 5. Execute order order_resp = execute_tool( url=f"{base_url}/orders", method="POST", headers={ "Authorization": f"Bearer {access_token}", "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body=json.dumps(order_payload) ) if order_resp.status_code == 201: print(f"Order placed! ID: {order_resp.json()['order_id']}") else: print(f"Failed: {order_resp.text}") ``` --- ## Things to keep in mind | Issue | Mitigation | |-------|------------| | **Authentication** | Use sandbox credentials or obtain a developer key from McDonald’s partner portal. | | **Rate limits** | Respect `Retry-After` headers; implement exponential backoff. | | **Payment security** | Never transmit raw card numbers; use tokenization or PCI‑compliant payment gateway. | | **Location accuracy** | Verify the store ID matches your delivery area; some APIs reject orders outside their service zone. | | **Legal compliance** | Ensure you’re authorized to use the API; many corporate APIs are restricted to partners only. | --- ### Bottom line 1. **Search** → find the official ordering API spec. 2. **Parse** → extract base URL, auth flow, and order schema. 3. **Build** → assemble a compliant JSON payload with the right product IDs. 4. **Execute** → call the order endpoint and handle the response. That’s the end‑to‑end recipe for turning a simple “burger + fries” request into a live order using the two tools you mentioned.
